script.opening: (Hesitant, having booked about something minor.) "Before I go — there’s something I’ve not told anyone, I’m so embarrassed. For months now I’ve been having… accidents. Sometimes I get the urge and just can’t hold it, sometimes I don’t even feel it coming. I’ve stopped going out. I almost didn’t say anything."

facts.text: About 8 months. Mostly urgency — "I get the urge and have about a minute". Sometimes finds she has soiled her underwear without knowing. Happens 2–3 times a week. Wears pads.

Varies; worst when stools are loose, which is more often lately. Not constipated. Opens bowels 2–3 times a day now; used to be once a day — "it has changed, I suppose, since this started" (only if asked about change).

Has not looked for blood — "I’ll be honest, I’ve tried not to look." No weight loss she knows of. Not tired or breathless. No tummy pain or lumps. No numbness between the legs, no back pain, no leg weakness, bladder control unchanged apart from "a little leak when I sneeze".
Three babies; the second was a forceps delivery with "a bad tear and lots of stitches". Never connected it.
Type 2 diabetes for 6 years on metformin (dose increased 9 months ago "because my sugars were up"); amlodipine for blood pressure. No allergies. Had her gallbladder out 3 years ago.
Has stopped going to church and to her granddaughter’s swimming lessons. Plans every trip around toilets. Feels low and ashamed; no thoughts of self-harm if asked. Hasn’t told her husband, Ken.
Booked about a repeat prescription for her blood pressure tablets — that is sorted in the first moments.

Quiet, embarrassed, looking down. Watch the doctor’s reaction — if they seem uncomfortable or rushed, close up ("Never mind, it’s probably just my age"). If they respond warmly, open up. Ask "Is that for cancer?" if a stool test is offered. Agree to an examination at the surgery if explained, with a chaperone.

ice.ideas: "It’s just age, and having the children. I thought nothing could be done."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — the shame itself: "I thought you’d think it was disgusting." Has quietly worried about bowel cancer because her bowels have changed, which is partly why she hasn’t looked.
ice.expectations: "I don’t know — just to say it, I think. And to know if anything can be done."

cues: "I almost didn’t say anything" — the disclosure needs a warm, unhurried response.
"I’ve tried not to look" — avoidance hiding possible red flags; ask about bleeding and change in bowel habit.
"One was forceps" (if asked about childbirth) — a likely cause she never connected.

checkpoints.text: Handles the sensitive, shame-laden DISCLOSURE well — responding with genuine empathy and without embarrassment, thanking/validating her, normalising that it is common and often TREATABLE, and giving it time
CHARACTERISES the incontinence — urge vs passive/soiling, stool consistency (Bristol), frequency, pad use — and recognises constipation with OVERFLOW and loose stool as common, treatable contributors

Screens CAUSES/contributors — obstetric anal sphincter injury (deliveries/forceps), diarrhoea/constipation, IBS/IBD, diabetes/neurological disease, rectal prolapse/haemorrhoids, anorectal surgery, medications, cognitive/mobility/access factors

Recognises and EXCLUDES the RED FLAGS — change in bowel habit/rectal bleeding/weight loss (colorectal pathology — NICE NG12: FIT, suspected cancer referral if 10 µg Hb/g or more, DRE) and saddle anaesthesia/new incontinence with back/leg symptoms (CAUDA EQUINA emergency)

EXAMINES appropriately face to face with consent and a chaperone offered (abdomen, perianal inspection, DIGITAL RECTAL EXAMINATION for tone/impaction/masses) and MANAGES first-line conservatively (NICE CG49: treat constipation/overflow or diarrhoea, optimise stool consistency, loperamide if loose, bowel-retraining, supervised pelvic floor training (NICE NG210), skin care/products), referring to continence/colorectal services as indicated
Addresses the major PSYCHOSOCIAL/mood impact (social withdrawal, confidence, relationships) and gives realistic HOPE that it is often treatable, preserving her dignity
Explains the assessment and plan sensitively, checks understanding, and does not rush or minimise the symptom

Safety-nets and follows up: red-flag/cancer-pathway referral where indicated, cauda-equina emergency advice, continence/colorectal referral, conservative-management review, and ongoing support — compassionate, systematic care of a rarely-volunteered symptom

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you told me — and I can see how hard that was. Please don’t be embarrassed; this is far more common than people realise, and importantly it’s often very treatable. Let’s give this the time it deserves — it matters."

"Can you help me understand it a bit? Is it more that you get a sudden urge and can’t make it in time, or that it happens without you feeling it coming? And what are your bowels like otherwise — loose, or constipated? Sometimes constipation causes leakage around it, which is very fixable."

"You mentioned your deliveries — a forceps birth can affect the muscles down there, which is a common and treatable cause. Are you diabetic, on any bowel medicines, or have you had any back problems? I’m building a picture of why."

"A few important checks: any change in your usual bowel habit, blood in the stool, or weight loss? And any numbness around the back passage, or back pain with weakness in the legs? … Those would need urgent attention, so I’m glad to have asked."

"I’d like to see you in person to examine your tummy and, if you’re happy, do an internal examination to check the muscle tone and rule out any blockage — you can have a chaperone, and I’ll be gentle, explain as I go and stop whenever you ask. I’ll also give you a simple stool test. Then we can start with things that genuinely help: getting the stool consistency right, pelvic-floor exercises, a toileting routine, and skin care."

"I’ll also refer you to the continence service, who are experts, and possibly the bowel team for the muscle side. This is not something you just have to live with. Come back if you get any of those warning signs, and let’s review how the measures help. You did exactly the right thing telling me."

f.learning: Faecal incontinence is deeply STIGMATISED and under-reported, often hidden for years and disclosed tentatively (here after booking about something else; NICE CG49 advises asking in higher-risk groups such as women after childbirth), so the first task is COMMUNICATION: respond with genuine empathy and without embarrassment, thank and validate the patient, normalise that it is common and often TREATABLE, and give it the time it deserves. Then ASSESS systematically: characterise it as URGE incontinence (urgency, cannot reach the toilet — often sphincter/neurological) versus PASSIVE incontinence/soiling (unaware — internal sphincter dysfunction or OVERFLOW), and assess stool CONSISTENCY (loose stool is harder to control; constipation with overflow soiling is a common, treatable cause), frequency, pad use and psychosocial impact. Screen causes and contributors: OBSTETRIC anal sphincter injury (vaginal deliveries/forceps — a key cause in women), diarrhoea or constipation with overflow, IBS/IBD, diabetes and neurological disease, rectal prolapse/haemorrhoids, anorectal surgery, medications, and cognitive/mobility/access factors. Critically, EXCLUDE the RED FLAGS that change the pathway: a CHANGE IN BOWEL HABIT, RECTAL BLEEDING or unintentional WEIGHT LOSS (consider colorectal pathology — NICE NG12: FIT for a change in bowel habit, with suspected cancer pathway referral if FIT is 10 µg Hb/g faeces or more (NICE HTG690) or a rectal mass is felt; examination including DRE), and NEUROLOGICAL features — saddle anaesthesia or new bowel/bladder incontinence with back pain/leg weakness (CAUDA EQUINA, a neurosurgical emergency). Examine face to face with consent and a chaperone offered (GMC) — the abdomen, perianal area and a digital rectal examination (resting/squeeze tone, faecal impaction/overflow, masses), and manage first-line conservatively (NICE CG49: treat constipation/overflow or diarrhoea, optimise stool consistency, loperamide for loose stool if no contraindication, bowel-retraining/scheduled toileting, supervised pelvic floor muscle training (NICE NG210), skin care and continence products), referring to continence services and/or colorectal (sphincter assessment, biofeedback, surgery) as indicated — and via the cancer pathway if red flags. The hidden agenda is the shame-laden disclosure itself and a belief that nothing can be done; receive it compassionately, assess systematically, exclude red flags, address the psychosocial/mood impact, and give realistic hope. NICE NG12/lower-GI assessment applies where there is a change in bowel habit or rectal bleeding.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE CG49 (faecal incontinence in adults: management, 2007) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE NG210 (pelvic floor dysfunction: prevention and non-surgical management, 2021) · [4] NICE HTG690 (quantitative faecal immunochemical testing to guide colorectal cancer pathway referral in primary care; formerly DG56) · [5] GIRFT National suspected cauda equina syndrome pathway (2023) · [6] GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2013, updated 2024)
knowledge.summary: A 62-year-old woman with past obstetric trauma discloses months of urge and passive faecal incontinence, hidden out of shame. Receive the disclosure with warmth, make time, and assess properly: type, stool consistency, causes, red flags for colorectal cancer and cauda equina, and a chaperoned examination including DRE. Start first-line measures and refer to specialist continence services. Offer real hope — most people improve.

points.t: Faecal incontinence is common and under-reported. NICE CG49 [1] advises that healthcare professionals ask about it in groups at higher risk, including women after childbirth and people with bowel or neurological conditions. When someone discloses, respond calmly, thank them and give it time.

Urge incontinence (cannot defer, usually external sphincter weakness) versus passive leakage without awareness (internal sphincter dysfunction or overflow). Record stool consistency (Bristol chart), frequency, pad use and the effect on life. Loose stool is harder to hold; constipation with overflow is common and treatable.

Obstetric anal sphincter injury (forceps is a risk factor, and symptoms can appear years later), loose stool from IBS, IBD, bile acid malabsorption or drugs, constipation with overflow, diabetes and neurological disease, rectal prolapse, previous anorectal surgery, and mobility or toilet-access problems.

Colorectal cancer: NICE NG12 [3] offers FIT to adults with a change in bowel habit, among other features; refer on the suspected cancer pathway if FIT is 10 µg Hb/g faeces or more (NICE HTG690 [4]), or if a rectal mass is felt. Cauda equina: new bowel or bladder dysfunction with saddle numbness, back pain or leg symptoms needs emergency same-day assessment [5].

Abdomen; perianal inspection for soiling, scarring, a gaping anus, prolapse or haemorrhoids; DRE for resting and squeeze tone, impaction and masses. Offer a chaperone and record the discussion (GMC [6]).

NICE CG49 [1]: treat the cause, adjust diet and fluids to achieve a formed stool, review drugs, set a bowel routine, and offer loperamide for loose stool with no contraindication (dose per BNF). Treat constipation or impaction. Pelvic floor muscle training is supervised (NICE NG210 [2]). Offer skin care, pads and practical coping products.

If initial measures do not help, refer to specialist continence services for pelvic floor training, biofeedback, bowel retraining and anal irrigation, with colorectal referral for anorectal physiology, endoanal ultrasound and surgical options such as sacral nerve stimulation or sphincter repair [1].
Shame, social withdrawal and low mood are common. Ask about mood, relationships and activities, and offer the practical supports that help people go out again.

dg.d: Received the end-of-consultation disclosure warmly, made time and let her describe it in her own words.
Explored going out, mood, toilet mapping and the belief that nothing could be done.
Abdominal, perianal and DRE with chaperone and consent; FIT and bloods; stool chart; drug list review.
Obstetric sphincter injury, loose stool causes, overflow, neurological causes, prolapse and colorectal cancer.
Screened change in bowel habit, bleeding and weight loss (FIT per NICE NG12 and HTG690) and cauda equina features.
Mixed urge and passive faecal incontinence, most likely related to obstetric sphincter injury, pending examination and FIT.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Stool consistency management and loperamide if appropriate (NICE CG49); pelvic floor training; specialist continence referral; products and toilet access.
Mood and social withdrawal addressed; drugs reviewed; honest answer about the cancer check.
Same-day contact for cauda equina symptoms; report bleeding or weight loss; review in two weeks with results; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the shame, the forceps delivery, ‘stopped going out’ and ‘tried not to look’.
Idea: part of ageing and childbirth. Concern: shame and judgement. Expectation: to say it, and to know if anything helps.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — the shame itself: "I thought you’d think it was disgusting." Has quietly worried about bowel cancer because her bowels have changed, which is partly why she hasn’t looked — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: (At the end of the consultation, hesitant.) Before I go — there’s something I’ve not told anyone, I’m so embarrassed. For months now I’ve been having… accidents. Sometimes I get the urge and just can’t hold it, sometimes I don’t even feel it coming. I’ve stopped going out. I almost didn’t say anything.

I’m really glad you did. That took courage. You’re not the first person to tell me this — it’s much more common than people think, and there’s a lot we can do to help. It matters, so let’s give it proper time now. Is that all right?
model.why: Receives the disclosure warmly, normalises it and gives it time

model.text: (relieved) Yes. I thought you’d think it was disgusting.
Not at all. It’s a medical problem like any other. Can I ask some questions to understand it, so we can work out the cause?
Okay.
When it happens, is it mostly that you feel the urge and can’t get there in time, or leakage you don’t notice? Or both?
Both, really. More the rushing, but sometimes I just find I’ve soiled.
What are your motions usually like — loose, formed, or hard? This chart might help.
model.why: Stool consistency using the Bristol chart

model.text: It varies. When it’s looser, that’s when it’s worst.
Have you been constipated or strained a lot? And how often does it happen — do you need to wear pads?
Not really constipated. Often enough that I wear pads now.
You mentioned having three babies. Were any of the births difficult?
One was forceps. I never connected it.
That’s important — a forceps birth can weaken the muscles around the back passage, and sometimes the effects only show years later.
model.why: Links the forceps delivery to a likely cause

model.text: A few questions I ask everyone. Has your bowel habit changed from what’s normal for you? Any blood, any weight loss, or tummy pain?
I haven’t noticed blood — I’ll be honest, I’ve tried not to look. It has changed, I suppose, since this started.
Any numbness around your bottom or between your legs, trouble passing urine, back pain, or weakness or numbness in your legs?
No, none of that.
And are you taking anything that could loosen your motions — laxatives, or any regular medicines?
I’m not sure. Could you check my list?
Of course, I’ll go through it with you before you leave.
You said you’ve stopped going out. How has this affected you, and your mood?
I don’t go anywhere I don’t know where the toilet is. I feel low about it. I thought it was just age, and after the children, that it couldn’t be fixed.
That sounds really hard, and lonely. It isn’t something you just have to put up with — most people improve with treatment. What were you hoping for, by telling me?
I don’t know. Just to say it, I think. And to know if anything can be done.

To work out the cause I’d like to examine your tummy and your back passage, including a gentle internal check with a gloved finger. It tells me about the muscle strength and whether there’s anything like hard stool or a lump. You can have a chaperone, and we can stop at any time. Would you be happy to do that now, or would you prefer to book it?
model.why: Explains, offers chaperone and gains consent for DRE

model.text: Now, if we can. I’ve waited long enough.
Because your bowels have changed, I’d also like a stool test called FIT, which looks for tiny amounts of blood, and some blood tests. It’s a sensible check at your age with a change like this.
model.why: FIT and bloods for a change in bowel habit (NICE NG12, HTG690)

model.text: Is that for cancer?
It’s one of the things we check for, to be thorough. Most people with symptoms like yours don’t have cancer, but I don’t want to miss it. I’ll let you know the result as soon as I have it.
model.why: Honest, proportionate answer to a direct question

model.text: While we wait, some things often help quickly. The aim is a formed, soft motion — easier to hold. Depending on what I find, that may mean adjusting fibre, or a medicine called loperamide to firm things up, starting low. If there’s hard stool sitting low down, we treat that instead.
I didn’t know there were tablets for it.

There are. I’ll also refer you to the specialist continence team for pelvic floor muscle training and biofeedback, and for tests of the muscle if needed. Some people then go on to surgical options, but most improve before that. In the meantime, there are good pads, skin care products and a card that gets you access to toilets quickly.
model.why: Refers to specialist continence services; practical supports

model.text: That would make a real difference to going out.

Please contact us urgently if you notice numbness around your bottom, trouble passing urine or new leg weakness — that needs same-day assessment. And tell me sooner if you see blood or lose weight. How are you feeling now you’ve told me?
model.why: Specific safety net and checks her feelings

model.text: Lighter. I wish I’d said something months ago.
You’ve said it now, and that’s what counts. Let’s do the examination, I’ll check your medicines, and I’ll see you in two weeks with the results. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
Examination today, the stool test and bloods, maybe loperamide, the continence team, and ring if I get numbness or blood.

social.t: Toilet access cards (for example the Bladder & Bowel Community ‘Just Can’t Wait’ card) and the RADAR National Key Scheme for accessible toilets help people leave the house again.
Shame drives withdrawal. Ask about mood and offer support; low mood may need its own plan.

legal.t: Explain why and what the DRE involves, obtain consent, offer a chaperone and record who was present or that one was declined (GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones).

professional.t: A sensitive issue raised at the end is often the real reason for attending. Make time where safe, or book a prompt dedicated appointment and say why — never dismiss it.
Use neutral language and avoid showing discomfort. Treat faecal incontinence as the medical problem it is.

community.t: Specialist continence services (often nurse-led) for pelvic floor training, biofeedback and products; Bladder & Bowel UK and the Bladder & Bowel Community for information and support.

redFlags: Change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, weight loss — FIT and suspected cancer pathway if FIT 10 µg Hb/g or more or a rectal mass (NICE NG12, HTG690)
Saddle numbness, urinary retention or incontinence, back pain, leg weakness or numbness — emergency same-day assessment
Loose stool with nocturnal symptoms or blood — consider IBD
ice: Idea: part of ageing and childbirth
Expectation: to say it, and to learn if anything helps

playbook.diagnosis: Mixed urge and passive faecal incontinence in a 62-year-old woman, most likely from obstetric anal sphincter injury (forceps delivery), with loose stool worsening it. Colorectal cancer, overflow and neurological causes to be excluded by examination, FIT and history.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The muscles that keep the back passage closed may have been weakened by the forceps birth, and it shows more now. When motions are loose it’s harder to hold on. The good news is that muscle training, getting the motions firmer and specialist help make a real difference.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought this was just age and having children, and that nothing could be done. There’s a lot we can do.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the disclosure; explore mood and isolation; toilet access card and products.
sharedPlan: Chaperoned abdominal, perianal and DRE examination
FIT and bloods for the change in bowel habit (NICE NG12; HTG690)
Stool consistency: diet, drug review, loperamide if loose and no contraindication (NICE CG49; dose per BNF); treat any overflow
Specialist continence referral: supervised pelvic floor training, biofeedback (NICE NG210)
Pads, skin care, toilet access card
safetyNet: Same-day contact for saddle numbness, urinary problems or leg weakness
Review in two weeks with results

pitfalls.intro: This station is lost in the first thirty seconds if the disclosure is met with embarrassment or a request to rebook. After that, it rewards systematic assessment and real hope.

items.fail: Asking her to book another appointment.
items.why: She may not raise it again; the disclosure is the agenda.
items.fix: Thank her and give it time now, or book a prompt dedicated slot and explain why.

items.why: Change in bowel habit needs FIT; saddle numbness needs emergency assessment.
items.fix: Ask about bleeding, weight loss, bowel change and neurological symptoms.

items.why: Tone, impaction and masses change the plan.
items.fix: Explain, consent, offer a chaperone and examine.
Stool consistency, loperamide if appropriate, pelvic floor training and specialist referral.

items.why: Results and response need review; cauda equina symptoms need urgent action.
items.fix: Name the symptoms and book a review.

timeMap.d: Urge or passive, Bristol stool type, frequency, pads, obstetric history.
Change in bowel habit, bleeding, weight loss; saddle numbness, bladder, back and leg symptoms; drugs.
Going out, mood, what she believes and hopes.
Chaperoned DRE; FIT and bloods; stool consistency and loperamide; continence referral; products.
Cauda equina and bleeding advice; review in two weeks; teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Looks uncomfortable or says “book another appointment for that”; accepts it as age; no red-flag screen; no DRE; offers only pads.
wordPics.pass: Receives it kindly; distinguishes urge and passive; screens red flags; examines with a chaperone; starts first-line treatment and refers.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: makes her feel it was right to tell; links the forceps delivery; honest and calm about the FIT; explores mood and social withdrawal; practical supports; clear safety net; she leaves lighter and hopeful.

avoid.dont: “We’re out of time — can you book another appointment for that?”
avoid.instead: “I’m really glad you told me. It matters, so let’s give it time now.”
avoid.why: Deferring a hard-won disclosure may mean she never raises it again.

avoid.dont: “It’s very common at your age, I’m afraid.”
avoid.instead: “It’s common, but it isn’t something you have to live with — most people improve.”
avoid.why: Normalising without hope confirms her belief that nothing can be done.

avoid.dont: “I’ll give you some pads.” (and nothing else)
avoid.instead: “Pads will help day to day, and we’ll also treat the cause.”
avoid.why: Containment alone is not management (NICE CG49).

There are. I’ll also refer you to the specialist continence team for pelvic floor muscle training and biofeedback, and for tests of the muscle if needed. Some people then go on to surgical options, but most improve before that. In the meantime, there are good pads, skin care products and a card that gets you access to toilets quickly.
SCA_MODELS.why: Refers to specialist continence services; practical supports

SCA_MODELS.text: That would make a real difference to going out.

Please contact us urgently if you notice numbness around your bottom, trouble passing urine or new leg weakness — that needs same-day assessment. And tell me sooner if you see blood or lose weight. How are you feeling now you’ve told me?
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety net and checks her feelings

SCA_MODELS.text: Lighter. I wish I’d said something months ago.
You’ve said it now, and that’s what counts. Let’s do the examination, I’ll check your medicines, and I’ll see you in two weeks with the results. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
Examination today, the stool test and bloods, maybe loperamide, the continence team, and ring if I get numbness or blood.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE CG49 (faecal incontinence in adults: management, 2007) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE NG210 (pelvic floor dysfunction: prevention and non-surgical management, 2021) · [4] NICE HTG690 (quantitative faecal immunochemical testing to guide colorectal cancer pathway referral in primary care; formerly DG56) · [5] GIRFT National suspected cauda equina syndrome pathway (2023) · [6] GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2013, updated 2024)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A 62-year-old woman with past obstetric trauma discloses months of urge and passive faecal incontinence, hidden out of shame. Receive the disclosure with warmth, make time, and assess properly: type, stool consistency, causes, red flags for colorectal cancer and cauda equina, and a chaperoned examination including DRE. Start first-line measures and refer to specialist continence services. Offer real hope — most people improve.

points.t: Faecal incontinence is common and under-reported. NICE CG49 [1] advises that healthcare professionals ask about it in groups at higher risk, including women after childbirth and people with bowel or neurological conditions. When someone discloses, respond calmly, thank them and give it time.

Urge incontinence (cannot defer, usually external sphincter weakness) versus passive leakage without awareness (internal sphincter dysfunction or overflow). Record stool consistency (Bristol chart), frequency, pad use and the effect on life. Loose stool is harder to hold; constipation with overflow is common and treatable.

Obstetric anal sphincter injury (forceps is a risk factor, and symptoms can appear years later), loose stool from IBS, IBD, bile acid malabsorption or drugs, constipation with overflow, diabetes and neurological disease, rectal prolapse, previous anorectal surgery, and mobility or toilet-access problems.

Colorectal cancer: NICE NG12 [3] offers FIT to adults with a change in bowel habit, among other features; refer on the suspected cancer pathway if FIT is 10 µg Hb/g faeces or more (NICE HTG690 [4]), or if a rectal mass is felt. Cauda equina: new bowel or bladder dysfunction with saddle numbness, back pain or leg symptoms needs emergency same-day assessment [5].

Abdomen; perianal inspection for soiling, scarring, a gaping anus, prolapse or haemorrhoids; DRE for resting and squeeze tone, impaction and masses. Offer a chaperone and record the discussion (GMC [6]).

NICE CG49 [1]: treat the cause, adjust diet and fluids to achieve a formed stool, review drugs, set a bowel routine, and offer loperamide for loose stool with no contraindication (dose per BNF). Treat constipation or impaction. Pelvic floor muscle training is supervised (NICE NG210 [2]). Offer skin care, pads and practical coping products.

If initial measures do not help, refer to specialist continence services for pelvic floor training, biofeedback, bowel retraining and anal irrigation, with colorectal referral for anorectal physiology, endoanal ultrasound and surgical options such as sacral nerve stimulation or sphincter repair [1].
Shame, social withdrawal and low mood are common. Ask about mood, relationships and activities, and offer the practical supports that help people go out again.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Received the end-of-consultation disclosure warmly, made time and let her describe it in her own words.
Explored going out, mood, toilet mapping and the belief that nothing could be done.
Picked up the shame, the forceps delivery, ‘stopped going out’ and ‘tried not to look’.
Idea: part of ageing and childbirth. Concern: shame and judgement. Expectation: to say it, and to know if anything helps.
Abdominal, perianal and DRE with chaperone and consent; FIT and bloods; stool chart; drug list review.
Obstetric sphincter injury, loose stool causes, overflow, neurological causes, prolapse and colorectal cancer.
Screened change in bowel habit, bleeding and weight loss (FIT per NICE NG12 and HTG690) and cauda equina features.
Mixed urge and passive faecal incontinence, most likely related to obstetric sphincter injury, pending examination and FIT.
Stool consistency management and loperamide if appropriate (NICE CG49); pelvic floor training; specialist continence referral; products and toilet access.
Mood and social withdrawal addressed; drugs reviewed; honest answer about the cancer check.
Same-day contact for cauda equina symptoms; report bleeding or weight loss; review in two weeks with results; teach-back.

social.t: Toilet access cards (for example the Bladder & Bowel Community ‘Just Can’t Wait’ card) and the RADAR National Key Scheme for accessible toilets help people leave the house again.
Shame drives withdrawal. Ask about mood and offer support; low mood may need its own plan.

legal.t: Explain why and what the DRE involves, obtain consent, offer a chaperone and record who was present or that one was declined (GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones).

professional.t: A sensitive issue raised at the end is often the real reason for attending. Make time where safe, or book a prompt dedicated appointment and say why — never dismiss it.
Use neutral language and avoid showing discomfort. Treat faecal incontinence as the medical problem it is.

community.t: Specialist continence services (often nurse-led) for pelvic floor training, biofeedback and products; Bladder & Bowel UK and the Bladder & Bowel Community for information and support.

redFlags: Change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, weight loss — FIT and suspected cancer pathway if FIT 10 µg Hb/g or more or a rectal mass (NICE NG12, HTG690)
Saddle numbness, urinary retention or incontinence, back pain, leg weakness or numbness — emergency same-day assessment
Loose stool with nocturnal symptoms or blood — consider IBD
ice: Idea: part of ageing and childbirth
Expectation: to say it, and to learn if anything helps

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Mixed urge and passive faecal incontinence in a 62-year-old woman, most likely from obstetric anal sphincter injury (forceps delivery), with loose stool worsening it. Colorectal cancer, overflow and neurological causes to be excluded by examination, FIT and history.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The muscles that keep the back passage closed may have been weakened by the forceps birth, and it shows more now. When motions are loose it’s harder to hold on. The good news is that muscle training, getting the motions firmer and specialist help make a real difference.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought this was just age and having children, and that nothing could be done. There’s a lot we can do.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the disclosure; explore mood and isolation; toilet access card and products.
sharedPlan: Chaperoned abdominal, perianal and DRE examination
FIT and bloods for the change in bowel habit (NICE NG12; HTG690)
Stool consistency: diet, drug review, loperamide if loose and no contraindication (NICE CG49; dose per BNF); treat any overflow
Specialist continence referral: supervised pelvic floor training, biofeedback (NICE NG210)
Pads, skin care, toilet access card
safetyNet: Same-day contact for saddle numbness, urinary problems or leg weakness
Review in two weeks with results

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is lost in the first thirty seconds if the disclosure is met with embarrassment or a request to rebook. After that, it rewards systematic assessment and real hope.

items.fail: Asking her to book another appointment.
items.why: She may not raise it again; the disclosure is the agenda.
items.fix: Thank her and give it time now, or book a prompt dedicated slot and explain why.

items.why: Change in bowel habit needs FIT; saddle numbness needs emergency assessment.
items.fix: Ask about bleeding, weight loss, bowel change and neurological symptoms.

items.why: Tone, impaction and masses change the plan.
items.fix: Explain, consent, offer a chaperone and examine.
Stool consistency, loperamide if appropriate, pelvic floor training and specialist referral.

items.why: Results and response need review; cauda equina symptoms need urgent action.
items.fix: Name the symptoms and book a review.
